title: Tortelloni di ricotta
subtitle: Large hand-formed ricotta and lemon pasta parcels
excerpt: Large, square fresh pasta parcels filled with ricotta, lemon zest, and Parmesan, sealed into plump cushions and served with brown butter and sage. Tortelloni, not tortellini: the larger, vegetarian cousin.
sourceNotes: Tortelloni di ricotta is a classic of the Emilia-Romagna tradition. The dish is documented in Pellegrino Artusi's La Scienza in Cucina e l'Arte di Mangiar Bene (1891, public domain) and appears in the broader canon of Bolognese stuffed pasta. Unlike tortellini (which have a meat filling and are ring-shaped), tortelloni are larger and typically filled with ricotta. The dish is described in detail in Waverly Root's The Food of Italy (1971) and in multiple Italian regional pasta cookbooks.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze on a floured tray until solid, then transfer to a bag. Cook from frozen: add 2 minutes to the cooking time.
recipe.batchNotes: Makes a large batch efficiently. Double the recipe and freeze half.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Assembled tortelloni can be refrigerated on a floured tray, loosely covered, for up to 4 hours before cooking.

content.text: Tortelloni are the bigger, less fussy cousin of tortellini: square parcels rather than rings, filled with ricotta rather than meat. The filling is simple (ricotta, Parmesan, lemon zest, and a little nutmeg) and comes together quickly while the pasta rests. The sauce is always some form of butter. Brown butter with sage is the classic. A simple melted butter and Parmesan is equally good.

items.prepNote: drained in a sieve for 30 minutes

content.text: Mound the flour on a clean work surface. Make a well in the centre and crack in the eggs. Beat the eggs with a fork, gradually working in the flour from the edges. When a shaggy dough forms, knead by hand for 8 to 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. The dough should feel like soft leather. Wrap in cling film and rest for 30 minutes at room temperature.
Mix the drained ricotta, Parmesan, lemon zest, and nutmeg together. Season with salt. Taste and adjust.
Divide the dough into quarters. Roll each quarter as thinly as possible (1 to 2 mm): the dough should be translucent. Keep unused pieces covered with a damp cloth to prevent drying.

Cut the rolled pasta into 7 cm squares. Place a heaped teaspoon of filling in the centre of each square. Brush the edges with a little water. Fold the pasta over the filling to make a rectangle, pressing out any air. Press the edges to seal firmly. Fold the long side up so the two pointed corners meet, press together, and curl slightly.
Alternatively, leave them as sealed rectangular parcels. Both shapes work. The simpler version is faster.
Arrange on a floured tray. Refrigerate for at least 30 minutes before cooking.
Brown the butter with the sage leaves over medium heat in a large frying pan until the butter smells nutty and the sage crisps. Keep warm over very low heat.

Cook the tortelloni in heavily salted, gently boiling water for 3 to 4 minutes until the pasta is tender and the filling is hot. Lift out with a slotted spoon or spider into the pan with the brown butter. Add a splash of pasta cooking water and toss gently. Serve immediately in warm bowls, scattered with grated Parmesan.

items.cause: Air trapped inside, or edges not sealed properly
items.fix: Press all air out before sealing. A well-sealed tortelloni feels plump but not taut. Press with your fingers along every edge.
Always drain ricotta before using. Wet ricotta makes a sloppy filling that leaks out.

content.text: Tortelloni di ricotta is a dish of the Po Valley: Emilia-Romagna and Lombardy. Unlike tortellini (a Bolognese speciality with a precise shape and a meat filling), tortelloni are more loosely defined. They appear in different forms across the region. The ricotta version is vegetarian and light. It is served at the start of a meal rather than as a main course. It is the kind of pasta that appears at Italian family tables on Sundays when the cook wants something special without the effort of a meat ragù.
